item.title: Gemini's New AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

Google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Gemini Task is a great way to manage your Inbox

Perhaps unsurprisingly, Gemini Task works well with Gmail, though even here there are some quirks. I created multiple automations to organize, manage, and automate spam deletion. First, I tackled the issue of marketing spam. I asked Gemini to locate marketing emails from the last week, unsubscribe from them on my behalf, and then to create a report on all the actions. Without my consent, it couldn’t unsubscribe from emails, whether Gemini wanted to unsubscribe from one email or 10. In addition, there was no way to individually uncheck email newsletters I wanted to keep. While I agreed to unsubscribe from some batches it suggested, I skipped others, like a group of 10 emails that contained a couple of messages from my bank. After the task was complete, I got a nicely formatted report in Google Sheets.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Use Gemini Task to replace third-party subscription managers

Gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

Gemini Task struggles on the open web

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

Gemini's free plan comes with some constraints

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro users. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

Some features, though, are only for U.S. users. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

It’s best to stay in the Google-verse

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any important steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free plan, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

item.title: When Gratitude Feels Like One More Thing You’re Failing At
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Every year as the holiday season approaches, gratitude advice arrives on cue. Count your blessings, says a friend. Write down three things you’re grateful for, urges a social media post. “Focus on the positive,” declares an advertisement, pitching the extra indulgence you oh-so deserve.

There’s plenty of wisdom in appreciating what’s good in our lives. But what happens when life feels difficult, and gratitude is the last thing on your mind?

When life is hard, being told to feel grateful can sound like the opposite of good advice. Not only are you struggling, but apparently you’re not appreciating your life properly either.

As a mindfulness teacher, I sometimes hear people share their difficulties after our morning meditation. They’re navigating loneliness, relationship problems, health issues, uncertainty about the future, or the loss of someone they love. At times like these, being told to feel grateful can sound like the opposite of good advice. Not only are you struggling, but apparently you’re not appreciating your life properly either.

item.title: The Best Early Tech Deals From Amazon’s 2026 Black Friday Sale
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: listicle, SEO round-up

Early Black Friday sales are in full swing at retailers like Sam's Club and Walmart, with deals to be found on brands like Apple and Samsung, and in categories from laptops to smartwatches—but one of the main places you should be looking is Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale.

I pored over this year's offerings and found many tech deals worth highlighting.

Amazon Smartwatch Black Friday Deals

CMF by Nothing Watch 3 Pro For $55 / Save $24

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount: Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

Amazon Headphone Black Friday Deals

Apple AirPods Pro 3 for $179 / Save $70

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds comes with a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation. They're $149 on Amazon (originally $249) as an early Black Friday deal.

Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) For $199 / Save $160

The Bose QuietComfort 2nd Gen is currently down to $199 (originally $359), its lowest price ever. The Bose QuietComfort line has been around for a long time, excelling in comfort, ANC, and minimalism. As PCMag mentions in their review, their sound profile leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Sony WH-1000XM6 for $378 / Save $81.99

The Sony WH-1000XM6 came out in 2025 and are the best over-ear headphones I tested last year (or ever, really). These headphones go with a companion app that's packed with a lot more features that you can nerd out on. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever.

Amazon Monitor and Laptop Black Friday Deals

Samsung 32-inch Odyssey G5 (G51F) for $179.99 / Save $120

Samsung’s 32-inch Odyssey G5 (G51F) gaming monitor has dropped to $179.99 on Amazon, which is the lowest price it has reached so far. It’s a flat panel (unlike Samsung’s many curved gaming displays), with a matte coating that helps minimize glare in brighter rooms, and comes with a stand that supports height, tilt, and pivot adjustments. The G51F’s combination of 180Hz refresh rate, 1ms response time, and AMD FreeSync support makes fast-paced games look smoother and feel more responsive than they do on standard 60Hz displays, especially in shooters, racing games, and competitive multiplayer titles.

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 15-inch (M5) For $1,249.99 / Save $249.01

If you're interested in the new M5 MacBook, Amazon is the only major retailer offering a $250 discount. The 15-inch MacBook Air is $1,199.99 (originally $1,499), and the new M5 chip is powerful enough to likely carry all of your workload without hiccups. Other sizes and configurations are also up to $300 off.

Amazon TV Black Friday Deals

Hisense 65-inch U6 Pro Mini-LED for $529.99 / Save $570

Budget TVs have improved dramatically over the years, and the Hisense U6 Series is a great example of what you can get today for a "budget" price. This is a QLED Mini LED TV, so while it's not at the quality that OLED TVs can offer, it makes up for it with a much lower price. Right now, the 65-inch Hisense Class U6 Series TV is $529.99 (originally $1,099.99), the lowest price it has been. Don't let the budget price fool you; this is a quality TV. The best one of 2025, according to PCMag's "outstanding" review. Its main attributes are its incredible levels of brightness, peaking at 1,024 nits, and its beautiful colors. This is expected from a QLED Mini LED TV, but not for under $550 for a 65-inch TV. It is also packed with features and specs that you won't find in other TVs at this price.

TCL 65-inch QM8L for $997.99 / Save $1,502

Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $997.99 (originally $2,499.99), its lowest price since it launched in April. The QM8L has a “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits; no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming, and contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

Hisense 65-inch E7 for $499.99 / Save $500

The Hisense E7SF QLED is in the low to mid-range of the OLED category, but with its 45% discount, the price is much lower. Amazon currently has the 65-inch E7SF QLED for $499.99 (originally $999.99), which is especially notable given this model came out in April of this year. The first thing you'll notice about the Hisense E7 is how thin and lightweight it is. It comes with four HDMI connections, one of which is an eARC connection so you can plug in a soundbar, and two with a native 144Hz refresh rate in game mode.

Amazon Black Friday FAQs

Does Amazon have Black Friday deals?

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.…
